questions.text: When you examined the SQL queries Hibernate was generating for your JPA relationships, what specific patterns or challenges did you notice that helped you understand the underlying database operations better?
questions.answer: The biggest thing I noticed was the N+1 problem. I had a User entity with a OneToMany list of expenses, and when I loaded ten users and printed their expenses, Hibernate fired one query for the users and then ten more queries, one per user. In the logs it was very clear. I fixed it using a JOIN FETCH query in the repository, and the count went down to a single query. I also noticed that the default fetch type for ManyToOne is eager, which was loading the category every time even when I did not need it, so I changed it to lazy. Seeing the actual SQL made me realise that the ORM is not magic and I still need to think about the database.

questions.text: Can you explain the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList in Java and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.answer: ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array, so getting an element by index is fast, O(1). LinkedList is a doubly linked list, so getting by index is O(n) because it has to walk the nodes. Adding at the end is fast in both, although ArrayList sometimes has to resize and copy the array. Inserting or removing in the middle is O(n) for ArrayList because elements shift, and for LinkedList the actual link change is O(1) but you first have to find the position. In practice I would choose ArrayList almost always because it is more cache friendly and uses less memory. I would think about LinkedList only if I am mostly adding and removing at the ends, but then ArrayDeque is usually better anyway.
questions.feedback: You demonstrated a sophisticated grasp of Java collections by correctly identifying not just the Big-O complexities, but also the critical hardware-level factors like cache locality. To take your answer to the next level, explicitly mention that the 'O(1)' insertion for LinkedList only applies if you already hold a reference to the specific node, as that distinction is often the deciding factor in real-world implementations.
questions.modelAnswer: The primary difference lies in the underlying data structure: ArrayList uses a contiguous array, while LinkedList uses a series of nodes with pointers. You should choose ArrayList for scenarios requiring frequent random access, as it provides O(1) retrieval and better CPU cache performance due to memory contiguity. Conversely, LinkedList is theoretically superior for frequent insertions or deletions in the middle of the list, provided you already have an iterator at the target position to avoid the O(n) search time. In most practical applications, ArrayList is the default choice, and for queue-based operations, ArrayDeque is generally preferred over LinkedList due to its superior memory efficiency and performance.

questions.text: Could you elaborate more on the memory overhead differences between ArrayList and LinkedList, especially in terms of how this impacts performance in a high-throughput backend application?
questions.answer: Each element in a LinkedList is wrapped in a node object that has the value plus a previous and next pointer, so on a 64-bit JVM every element costs roughly 24 extra bytes plus the object header. ArrayList just stores references in one contiguous array, with some unused capacity at the end. So for a million items LinkedList uses noticeably more heap. In a high-throughput backend that means more garbage for the collector, and because nodes are scattered in memory the CPU cache misses a lot when you iterate. That is why even a plain loop over a LinkedList is usually slower than over an ArrayList. If I know the size in advance I would also create the ArrayList with an initial capacity to avoid repeated resizing.

I would choose a LinkedList only if the application logic requires frequent O(1) insertions or deletions at the beginning of the list, where the cost of shifting elements in an ArrayList would outweigh the memory overhead of the nodes.

questions.text: How would you implement a basic REST controller in Spring Boot that returns a list of products from a database? What annotations would you use?
questions.answer: I would create a Product entity with the @Entity annotation and an @Id field, and a ProductRepository interface that extends JpaRepository<Product, Long>, so I get findAll without writing SQL. Then a ProductService that calls the repository, and a ProductController annotated with @RestController and @RequestMapping("/api/products"). Inside it a method with @GetMapping that returns List<Product> from the service. Spring automatically converts the list to JSON using Jackson. I would inject the service through the constructor rather than @Autowired on the field, because it is easier to test. In a real app I would return a DTO instead of the entity, and add pagination with Pageable so it does not return thousands of rows at once.

questions.text: Explain the difference between REST and GraphQL APIs, including their advantages and disadvantages. When would you choose one over the other in a real-world application?
questions.answer: REST uses different URLs for different resources and HTTP methods like GET and POST. GraphQL has one endpoint and the client sends a query saying which fields it wants, so there is less over-fetching. REST is simpler and easier to cache. GraphQL is good when the frontend needs flexible data. I have only used REST in my projects so I would probably choose REST for most applications.

questions.modelAnswer: REST is resource-oriented, using standard HTTP verbs and status codes, which makes it highly cacheable and predictable for simple CRUD operations. GraphQL is query-oriented, allowing the client to request exactly the data it needs, which prevents over-fetching and reduces network overhead in complex applications. I would choose REST for public-facing APIs where standard caching and simplicity are priorities, whereas I would choose GraphQL for internal dashboards or mobile apps where the frontend requires highly specific, nested data structures that would otherwise require multiple REST round-trips.

questions.answer: During my internship, users of the internal reporting tool complained that some daily reports were missing rows. questions.text: You mentioned JWT authentication - how did you implement token expiration and refresh mechanisms in your Spring Security setup?
questions.answer: Honestly, expiration yes, refresh not yet. The access token is signed with HS256 and has a 30 minute expiry in the exp claim, and my JWT filter rejects expired tokens with a 401, so the frontend sends the user back to login. I know that is not ideal. The plan for refresh is a separate long-lived refresh token stored in an HttpOnly cookie and saved hashed in the database, with rotation, so each refresh issues a new one and invalidates the old one. Then logout or a stolen token can be revoked by deleting the row, which pure stateless JWTs cannot do.

questions.answer: One decision was how to store money. My first version used double for the amount, and I noticed summaries like 0.30000000000000004. questions.text: Could you elaborate on the performance characteristics of BigDecimal that made you comfortable with the trade-off between precision and speed in your financial calculations?
questions.answer: BigDecimal is an immutable object, so every addition creates a new object, and the arithmetic is done in software, so it is many times slower than adding primitive longs. But in my API a monthly summary adds at most a few hundred values per request, and the heavy aggregation actually happens in PostgreSQL with SUM on the NUMERIC column, not in Java. I measured the summary endpoint and it was dominated by the database round trip, not the arithmetic. If I had to process millions of transactions in memory, for example in a batch job, I would switch to long paise to avoid the object allocation.

questions.text: Tell me about a challenging bug or technical issue you encountered in your project, and how you approached debugging and solving it?
questions.answer: After deploying, users in India said expenses added late at night showed up in the wrong month's summary. I reproduced it by adding an expense at 11:30 pm IST. The server on Render runs in UTC, and I was storing a LocalDateTime without timezone and grouping by month in UTC, so 11:30 pm IST on the 31st became 6 pm UTC, which was fine, but anything after 5:30 am... actually the problem was the reverse: early morning entries on the 1st in IST were still the previous day in UTC. I fixed it by storing timestamps as timestamptz, accepting the user's timezone in their profile, and doing the month grouping in SQL with AT TIME ZONE. I added tests for boundary times on the first and last day of a month, and I now set the JVM default timezone explicitly to UTC so behaviour does not depend on the server.

questions.text: Explain the difference between HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap in Java, including when you would use each and the trade-offs involved.
questions.answer: HashMap is not thread-safe: if two threads write at the same time you can lose updates or corrupt the internal structure, so it's for single-threaded use or data confined to one thread. ConcurrentHashMap is built for concurrent access. Since Java 8 it uses CAS operations and locks only the bucket being written, so reads don't block and writes to different buckets run in parallel, which scales much better than Collections.synchronizedMap, which locks the whole map. It also gives atomic compound operations like computeIfAbsent and merge, which is how you safely do "increment this counter". Trade-offs: no null keys or values, iterators are weakly consistent rather than fail-fast, and size() is only an estimate under concurrent writes. So I use a plain HashMap inside a method or request, and ConcurrentHashMap for shared state like an in-memory cache or a rate-limit counter shared across request threads.
questions.feedback: You demonstrated a sophisticated understanding of how internal locking mechanisms impact performance and correctly identified the critical trade-offs regarding iterator consistency. To take your answer to the next level, try to briefly explain the 'why' behind the weak consistency of iterators, as this shows you understand the memory model implications of non-blocking data structures. You have a very strong grasp of these concepts, so keep focusing on how these internal design choices influence the behavior of the code in a multi-threaded environment.
questions.modelAnswer: A HashMap is designed for single-threaded environments where performance is prioritized over thread safety, as it lacks any synchronization mechanisms. In contrast, a ConcurrentHashMap is optimized for high-concurrency scenarios by using fine-grained locking and CAS operations, which allows multiple threads to read and write to different segments of the map simultaneously without blocking the entire structure. When choosing between them, I consider the scope of the data; if the map is local to a single thread or method, a HashMap is more efficient because it avoids the overhead of synchronization. However, if the map is shared across threads, such as in a global cache or a shared counter, ConcurrentHashMap is necessary to prevent race conditions. A key trade-off to keep in mind is that ConcurrentHashMap sacrifices strict consistency for performance, meaning iterators are weakly consistent and methods like size() provide an estimate rather than an exact count, which is a design choice that favors throughput over absolute precision.

questions.text: Could you explain how CAS operations work in ConcurrentHashMap and how they improve performance compared to traditional locking approaches?
questions.answer: CAS, compare-and-swap, is a single atomic CPU instruction: update this memory location to a new value only if it still holds the value I expect, otherwise fail so I can retry. ConcurrentHashMap uses it to insert into an empty bucket without taking any lock: the thread reads the slot as null and swaps in its new node only if it is still null. If another thread got there first the CAS fails and it retries or falls back to locking just that one bucket. Compared with locking the whole map, threads working on different keys never wait for each other, and there's no lock handoff or context switch on the common uncontended path, which is why it scales much better under many threads. The trade-off is that under heavy contention on the same key, retries add some wasted work.

You clearly understand the mechanics, so keep focusing on how these internal mechanisms interact with the JVM's memory model.

In a ConcurrentHashMap, this is used to perform lock-free updates on empty buckets; the thread checks if the bucket is null and attempts to swap in a new node in one atomic step. If the CAS fails because another thread modified the bucket, the thread simply retries or falls back to a synchronized block on that specific bucket node. This is significantly more performant than traditional locking because it avoids the overhead of thread suspension and context switching when there is no contention. I added the parallel script as an automated test, and during the college fest, with about two hundred bookings, we had zero double bookings.

questions.text: Imagine you're designing a REST API for an e-commerce platform. How would you approach versioning, error handling, and authentication? What are the trade-offs between different approaches?
questions.answer: Versioning: I'd put the major version in the URL, like /api/v1/orders, because it is explicit, easy to route and easy to cache, even though header-based versioning keeps URLs cleaner. I'd only bump the major version for breaking changes and keep additive changes, like a new optional field, in the same version, and support the old version for a deprecation period. Error handling: one consistent error format for every endpoint, for example the RFC 7807 problem-details shape with a type, title, status and a machine-readable code, produced by a single @ControllerAdvice, with correct status codes: 400 for validation, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 409 for conflicts like an out-of-stock item, and never leaking stack traces. Authentication: short-lived JWT access tokens with refresh-token rotation for the customer apps; the trade-off is that stateless JWTs are fast and scale horizontally but are hard to revoke, so the refresh token is stored server-side. For server-to-server calls, like the payment provider's webhooks, I'd verify signatures rather than use user tokens.

questions.text: You're given a database query that's performing poorly. How would you diagnose and optimize it? What tools and techniques would you use, and how would you ensure your changes don't introduce new issues?
questions.answer: First I'd measure, not guess: find the query in the slow-query log or pg_stat_statements, then run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the real plan, the row estimates versus actual rows, and where the time goes. Common findings are a sequential scan on a large table, which usually needs an index on the filter or join columns, ideally a composite index in the right column order; a bad row estimate, fixed by running ANALYZE to refresh statistics; or the N+1 pattern from the ORM, fixed with a join fetch or a batch query. Sometimes the fix is in the query itself, like avoiding a function on an indexed column, or adding pagination with keyset instead of a large OFFSET. To make sure I don't break anything, I'd test with production-like data volume, compare the results of the old and new query, check that a new index doesn't slow down writes too much, and create the index CONCURRENTLY through a Flyway migration so it doesn't lock the table. Then I'd confirm the improvement with the same metrics I started with.
questions.feedback: You demonstrated a sophisticated understanding of database internals by correctly prioritizing empirical measurement over guesswork and identifying specific anti-patterns like N+1 queries and inefficient pagination. To elevate your approach further, explicitly mention how you would use a staging environment to perform a 'before-and-after' comparison of execution plans to ensure your optimizations are objectively verified before deployment.

questions.text: If you were to build a new backend service for a real-time chat application, what would be your approach? Consider scalability, reliability, and security aspects.
questions.answer: I'd use WebSockets for the live connection, with a Spring Boot service handling connections and REST endpoints for history and room management. To scale horizontally, connections are spread over several instances behind a load balancer, and because two users in the same room may be on different instances, messages are published to a broker like Redis pub/sub or Kafka so every instance can deliver to its local connections. Messages are stored in a database partitioned by conversation and time, so loading the latest messages is a fast range query, with cursor pagination for scrolling back. For reliability, each message gets a client-generated id so retries are idempotent, the server acknowledges after persisting, and on reconnect the client asks for messages after its last seen id. For security, authenticate the WebSocket handshake with a short-lived token, check room membership on every send, rate-limit per user to stop spam, and use TLS everywhere. I'd start simpler, with one instance and Postgres, and add the broker once we actually need more than one instance.
